The Community Grant Program awards grants of $2,500 to $25,000 to 501(c)(3) nonprofits, entities with fiscal sponsorship, collaboratives with fiscal sponsors, houses of worship running community-serving programs that are not faith-based and do not proselytize, and large multiservice institutions applying for well-aligned discrete projects. Organizations must be based in Worcester County and serve primarily its residents, or have a meaningful physical presence there, or provide an unduplicated service in Worcester County with authentic partnerships and relationships with local stakeholders. Grants support discrete projects or programs aligned with one of five focus areas: Arts & Creativity (creative placemaking, intersectional arts and non-arts partnerships); Basic Needs (food, shelter, resources for permanency, household stabilization—excluding emergency/crisis funding); Economic Opportunity (English language learning, culturally responsive workforce programs); Health & Wellbeing (healthcare and social services navigation, complementary and palliative care, healthy pregnancies and strong starts); and Youth Development (innovative out-of-school programming, post-secondary support including workforce development and career readiness). Organizations must be in good financial standing with intact governance structures. Applications are assessed on feasibility, community access and inclusion, innovation and impact, clear goals and outcomes, commitment to equity, and organizational strength.

The Community Grant Program, administered by the Greater Worcester Community Foundation, awards close to $2 million annually across five strategic focus areas (Arts & Creativity, Basic Needs, Economic Opportunity, Health & Wellbeing, and Youth Development) for discrete project/programming support as well as general operating support; these guidelines cover the project support application. Grants range from $2,500 to $25,000, with partial grants possible, and may fund a pilot, a programmatic expansion, or support for an ongoing program. Eligible applicants include 501c3 nonprofits or entities operating under a 501c3 fiscal sponsor, collaboratives and coalitions with a fiscal sponsor and identified project lead, houses of worship running non-faith-based community programs, and large multiservice institutions applying for well-aligned discrete projects. Preference is given to organizations based in Worcester County serving primarily its residents, followed by organizations not based in the county but with a meaningful physical presence there, and then organizations providing an unduplicated service in Worcester County with demonstrated authentic local partnerships. Ineligible applicants include businesses, government organizations or municipalities, individuals (for scholarships, tuition, direct aid, etc.), projects occurring in classrooms during school time as part of academic curriculum, and requests for capital projects/campaigns. Basic needs programs cannot include emergency/crisis funding requests. Organizations must be in good financial standing with an intact governance structure, and applications are reviewed by Foundation staff and community volunteers based on feasibility, community access and inclusion, innovation and impact, clear goals and outcomes, commitment to equity, and organizational strength.

text: Hasbrofoundation Inc is a private foundation based in Pawtucket, RI, affiliated with Hasbro, whose purpose is to create joy and community for all people around the world through play. Its philanthropy focuses on Access to Play, bringing play to underserved and historically marginalized communities; Play Relief, providing support in times of crisis and uncertainty; and Play Makers, empowering the next generation. The foundation grants, with giving concentrated in Rhode Island, Florida, Washington DC, Connecticut, California, Massachusetts, New York, and Washington state. Typical grants range from $15,000 to $100,000, and the foundation gave $2,722,839 in 2024. It accepts applications from charitable organizations. Hasbro's Global Philanthropy and Social Impact program encompasses several initiatives: the Hasbro Foundation, which makes grants focused on delivering Access to Play to underserved and historically marginalized communities, providing Play Relief in times of crisis and uncertainty, and empowering the next generation of Play Makers; Gift of Play, a product donation program that provides toys and games to charitable organizations worldwide to bring joy, stability, and relief; Team Hasbro, an employee volunteer program; and Strategic Partners, partnerships leveraging Hasbro's business assets to support the same core focus areas of Access to Play, Play Relief, and Play Makers. The document is an overview landing page and does not provide specific award amounts, eligibility criteria, or application deadlines for any of these programs; it directs readers to separate pages for guidelines, policies, and strategy details. Hasbro's Global Philanthropy and Social Impact programming supports underserved and historically marginalized communities through local community grants in U.S. locations where Hasbro operates, focusing on three areas: Access to Play for underserved and historically marginalized communities, Play Relief in times of crisis and uncertainty, and empowering the next generation of Play Makers. Outside the U.S., Hasbro's global offices annually provide charitable support in the form of grants, sponsorships, product donations and/or volunteer engagement. All charitable support must benefit community members directly through a 501(c)3 nonprofit organization. Sponsorship support funds organizations in Hasbro's operating areas that deliver primary stability and health for children and families in crisis, skill development, and equitable access to education; Hasbro does not sponsor events such as 5ks, walks, or golf tournaments unless part of a companywide initiative with a Philanthropic Partner. Product donations must go directly into the hands of vulnerable children through a 501c3 non-profit child-focused organization, and are not permitted for fundraisers (raffles, auctions, carnivals), annual conferences/conventions, gift bags/door prizes, individuals, intermediary donations, or school incentive/reward programs. Holiday giving is managed through a partnership with Toys for Tots rather than direct organizational donations. All recipients must comply with Hasbro's Non-Discrimination Policy. Hasbro does not accept unsolicited donation requests, and is currently not accepting proposals for U.S. community grants. Impact reporting (quantitative and qualitative) is required at six-month and year-end timeframes for grant recipients to track outcomes.

A federal contracting and training program for experienced small business owners who are socially and economically disadvantaged. Certified participants receive business development assistance, access to set-aside and sole-source federal contracts, mentorship opportunities, and training to strengthen their ability to compete in the American economy.

The 8(a) program can be a valuable tool for experienced socially and economically disadvantaged small business owners, who have already been in business for at least two years or more, and are interested in expanding their footprint in the federal marketplace. The 8(a) program offers unique and valuable business assistance. The 8(a) certification does not guarantee contract awards but it is a dynamic tool to pursue and capture new opportunity from the government.

Certified firms in the 8(a) program can:

Efficiently compete and receive set-aside and sole-source contracts
Receive one-on-one business development assistance for their nine-year term from dedicated Business Opportunity Specialists focused on helping firms grow and accomplish their business objectives
Pursue opportunity for mentorship from experienced and technically capable firms through the SBA Mentor-Protégé program
Connect with procurement and compliance experts who understand regulations in the context of business growth, finance, and government contracting
Pursue joint ventures with established businesses to increase capacity
Qualify to receive federal surplus property on a priority basis
Receive free training from SBA’s Empower to Grow program
The 8(a) certification qualifies your business as eligible to compete for the program’s sole-source and competitive set-aside contracts. The government authorizes sole-source contracts to 8(a) participants for up to $7 million for acquisitions assigned manufacturing North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) codes and $4.5 million for all other acquisitions. Entity-owned 8(a) program participants are eligible for sole-source contracts above these thresholds, but the Department of Defense requires approval of a formal justification if the 8(a) sole-source contract exceeds $100 million; all other federal agencies require approval for sole-source 8(a) contract actions that exceed $25 million.

8(a) program participants are eligible to compete for contract awards under other socio-economic programs or small business set-asides they qualify for.

Program overview
Sections 7(j)(10) and 8(a) of the Small Business Act (15 U.S.C. §§ 636(j)(10) and 637(a)) authorizes the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) to establish a business development program, which is known as the 8(a) Business Development program. 

Businesses that participate in the program receive training and technical assistance designed to strengthen their ability to compete effectively in the American economy. Also eligible to participate in the 8(a) program are small businesses owned by Alaska Native corporations, Community Development Corporations, Indian tribes, and Native Hawaiian organizations. Small business development is accomplished by providing various forms of management, technical, financial, and procurement assistance.

SBA partners with federal agencies to promote maximum utilization of 8(a) program participants to ensure access to contracting opportunities in the federal marketplace. Once certified, 8(a) program participants are eligible to receive federal contracting and receive training and technical assistance designed to strengthen their ability to compete effectively in the American economy.

text: Community Care Corps is a national, federally funded grant program administered under a cooperative agreement between the Administration for Community Living (ACL) and a team led by the Oasis Institute, USAging, Caregiver Action Network and Altarum. The second 5-year cooperative agreement runs September 1, 2024 through August 31, 2029, and awards 18-month grants ranging from $30,000 to $200,000 to organizations across the country to develop, expand, or refine innovative community- and home-based volunteer programs that provide nonmedical assistance to family caregivers, older adults, and adults with disabilities age 18 and older so they can maintain independence in the community. The program anticipates funding between 23 and 27 new grantees each funding cycle; historically it has received 730 applications over 5 cycles and funded 132 grantees total. Eligible applicants include a wide range of non-profit entities such as local communities, non-profit organizations, state, county, and local governments, domestic public or private non-profit entities, Indian tribal governments and organizations, faith-based organizations, community-based organizations, hospitals, institutions of higher education, local aging service organizations as defined in the Older Americans Act, centers for independent living as defined in the Rehabilitation Act, entities with expertise in delivering such services, and time-banking or volunteer agencies. All applicants must be a 501(c)3 nonprofit (activated by the application due date) to apply, except that state and local governments are eligible even though they are not 501(c)3 organizations; organizations may not profit from the funds. Multiple chapters under one EIN/group 501(c)3 designation cannot apply separately, but a multi-location or multi-organization project may apply with one designated lead applicant, recipient and manager of award funds, submitting letters of commitment from partner organizations. Non-nonprofit applicants may partner with a nonprofit fiscal agent, which becomes the primary applicant subject to Uniform Guidance compliance and must have a Unique Entity ID and SAM.gov registration. All US states and territories, including Puerto Rico and the US Virgin Islands, are eligible. Current or past ACL grantees/applicants are not excluded. Funds must supplement, not supplant, existing funding and applicants should be able to meet a required match. Funding cannot be used for construction or rehabilitation of buildings (only minor home modifications/repairs promoting health and safety), income maintenance or financial assistance (e.g., rent, mortgage, utility relief), medical/health/personal care services, or ADA office renovations. Allowable uses include stipends, mileage reimbursement, snacks/meals for volunteers and participants, contracted personnel/drivers, tablets and Wi-Fi hotspots, marketing/promotional materials, background checks and fingerprinting, and volunteer liability insurance. Staff salary charged to the grant is capped at the Executive Level II rate ($225,700/year for 2025). All volunteers must be 18 or older and pass a criminal background check (with fingerprinting required for unsupervised direct contact); volunteers under 18 must be supervised and cannot have one-on-one interactions with care recipients. Grantees must carry volunteer liability insurance of at least $1 million per occurrence and $2 million aggregate before receiving funds, register in SAM.gov and obtain a Unique Entity ID, collect and report 12 months of data within the 18-month grant period (with up to 6 months for ramp-up), provide at least two videos per grant cycle and two written stories per quarter, and are reimbursed quarterly with 10% of federal funds provided upfront. Only one 18-month grant period is currently committed per grantee; federal funds are not secured beyond one cycle, so applicants should plan for sustainability.

The Irene E and George A Davis Foundation is a private foundation in Springfield, MA. Its 2024 tax filing reports $8,491,456 in grants, listed on an attachment the electronic filing does not include. Applicants must apply online and consult attached guidelines for restrictions, application procedures, and deadlines.

The Irene E. & George A. Davis Foundation invests in initiatives and organizations that help children, families, people, and communities in Hampden County, Massachusetts thrive, across six funding areas: Early Childhood, Youth Literacy, Innovation & Excellence in Education, Youth Development, Economic Development & Mobility, and Community Support. Organizations whose work directly benefits individuals living in Hampden County and whose activities align with one or more of these six funding areas may be eligible to apply.

The Irene E. & George A. Davis Foundation funds initiatives and organizations that help people and communities in Hampden County, Massachusetts thrive across six funding areas: Early Childhood, Youth Literacy, Innovation & Excellence in Education, Youth Development, Economic Development & Mobility, and Community Support. The Foundation does not fund work that does not serve or benefit individuals living in Hampden County or initiatives that lack multiple funding streams supporting the work. It rarely funds endowments, start-up organizations or projects that cannot provide at least one year of financial information on a full Form 990 (a 990-N or 990-EZ is not sufficient), or capital funding for facility construction, equipment purchases, or other physical capital improvements. Applicants must be a 501(c)(3) public charity or have a fiscal sponsor that is a 501(c)(3), must have filed a full Form 990 for the most recent fiscal year, and must have multiple funding sources. Proposed work must provide clear, practical benefits to Hampden County residents, demonstrate measurable outcomes or evidence of impact aligned with the Foundation's funding areas, and align with at least one of the six funding areas. Community Support grants are typically $25,000 or less; amounts for other funding areas are not specified in this document.

The Irene E. & George A. Davis Foundation accepts grant applications from organizations serving or impacting residents of Hampden County, Massachusetts. The Foundation's priority impact issue areas are Early Childhood, Youth Literacy, Innovation & Excellence in Education, Youth Development, and Economic Development & Mobility. Applicants must select the single funding area that best aligns with their work or proposed program. The Foundation also considers a 'Community Support' category for projects or programs that do not fit the priority areas but still provide a vital service to or enrich the lives of Hampden County residents; these Community Support grants are typically $25,000 or less. Applicants must identify which cities/towns in Hampden County their project impacts from a list including Agawam, Blandford, Brimfield, Chester, Chicopee, East Longmeadow, Granville, Hampden, Holland, Holyoke, Longmeadow, Ludlow, Monson, Montgomery, Palmer, Russell, Southwick, Springfield, Tolland, Wales, West Springfield, Westfield, and Wilbraham. Applicants must submit extensive organizational documentation including an IRS Determination Letter, most recent Form 990, three years of audited or reviewed financial statements, current fiscal year budget, leadership and board lists, and a list of top five funding sources over the past three years. The application requires narrative descriptions of the organization's mission and population served, the proposed project/program, target population and number served, program goals, measurement of success, and any available impact data. Applicants may optionally disclose other funders they have approached for the same project. Submission is subject to file attachment limits of up to 15 files and 30 MB combined across all uploads, and the application must be certified with the knowledge of the organization's Executive Director.

The Farm Storage Facility Loan Program (FSFL) provides low-interest financing so producers can build or upgrade permanent and portable storage facilities and equipment.

Eligible commodities include grains, oilseeds, peanuts, pulse crops, hay, hemp, honey, renewable biomass commodities, fruits and vegetables, floriculture, hops, maple sap, maple syrup, milk, cheese, yogurt, butter, eggs, meat/poultry (unprocessed), rye and aquaculture. Eligible facility types include grain bins, hay barns, bulk tanks, and facilities for cold storage.
Drying and handling and storage equipment is also eligible, including storage and handling trucks. Eligible facilities and equipment may be new or used, permanently affixed or portable.
Since its inception in May 2000, more than 33,000 loans have been issued for on-farm storage, increasing storage capacity by 900 million bushels.
FSFL is an excellent financing program for on-farm storage and handling for small and mid-sized farms, and for new farmers. Loan terms vary from 3 to 12 years.
The maximum loan amount for storage facilities is $500,000. The maximum loan amount for storage and handling trucks is $100,000.

In 2016 FSA introduced a new loan category, the microloan, for loans with an aggregate balance up to $50,000. Microloans offer a 5 percent down payment requirement, compared to a 15 percent down payment for a regular FSFL, and waive the regular three-year production history requirement.

The Farm Service Agency (FSA) administers the FSFL Program on behalf of the Commodity Credit Corporation (CCC). This rule amends the FSFL Program regulations to add eligibility for portable storage structures, portable equipment, and storage and handling trucks, and to reduce the down payment and documentation requirements for a new “microloan” category of FSFLs up to $50,000.
These changes are intended to address the needs of smaller farms and specialty crop producers.

The Terra Foundation Convening Grants support conversations, symposia, and workshops that stimulate interdisciplinary and intercultural exchange related to the visual arts of the United States and Indigenous arts of North America. Grants range from $10,000 to $25,000 and are awarded twice yearly. Eligible applicants include arts centers, community-based cultural organizations, foundations, museums, research centers, and universities of varying sizes and geographies, worldwide. Applicants must hold United States 501(c)(3) tax-exempt status or international equivalent; fiscal sponsorship is accepted for U.S.-based projects. Convenings may be in-person, virtual, or hybrid formats at any stage of project development. Grants support planning and implementation costs including professional fees, artist fees, travel, AV support, interpretation services, catering, research dissemination, marketing, and administrative costs (up to 20% of grant) and indirect costs (up to 15% of grant). Up to $5,000 may be used for publications within one year of the event. The primary focus must be anchored in visual arts; projects where U.S. visual arts and Indigenous North American arts are not central must clearly explain how the convening advances global dialogue or drives change in American art. The foundation prefers not to be the sole funder. Organizations that received a Terra grant within the previous two grant cycles are ineligible, though previously declined applicants may reapply.

The Terra Foundation for American Art's Convening Grants support convening programs (such as symposia, workshops, or public programs) that generate knowledge and interpretive frameworks reflecting the full breadth and complexity of American art and its histories, engage artists, scholars, and communities offering plural and intercultural/interdisciplinary perspectives, and catalyze inclusive practices and expansive histories in the field of American art. Applicants must be institutions with United States 501(c)(3) tax-exempt status or the international equivalent; organizations without their own tax-exempt status may apply through a fiscal sponsor that holds 501(c)(3) status. University museums should submit the museum's own budget rather than the university's. Convening Grants do not exceed $25,000 except in unusual circumstances. No more than 15% of the grant amount may be applied toward indirect costs, and up to 20% of a grant may offset direct administration costs. Up to $5,000 of an awarded grant may be used for resulting proceedings or publications (online or in print), and those funds must be spent within one year of the event. The Foundation has a preference for programs that are free of charge. Applicants must submit a detailed project budget using the Foundation's Convenings Budget Template, a budget narrative, and a list of secured, requested, and to-be-requested funders and amounts.

The Terra Foundation for American Art's Convening Grant supports organizations that host convening programs (such as symposia, conferences, or gatherings) focused on American art. The program is open to applicant organizations holding United States 501(c)(3) tax-exempt status or the international equivalent; organizations without their own tax-exempt status may apply through a fiscal sponsor that holds 501(c)(3) status. Applicants must describe their organizational history, purpose, goals and values, provide details of the convening program including start and end dates, content focus, format, and the individuals and any partner organizations developing it, and explain how the project addresses the program's three objectives: generating knowledge and interpretive frameworks reflecting the full breadth of American art and its histories, engaging artists, scholars, and communities representing plural perspectives and intercultural/interdisciplinary approaches, and catalyzing inclusive practices and expansive histories in the field of American art. University museums must submit the budget for the museum itself, not the university. The form requests a Grant Request Amount and Total Project Budget in USD, but no specific award ranges or caps are stated in the document.

Climatetech Pathmaker Grants fund short-term, industry-aligned training programs (8-12 weeks, 80-180 hours) that prepare individuals without significant industry experience for high-demand occupations in energy storage and power generation. The program provides up to $10,000 per employment outcome over one year through direct funding and technical assistance to eligible Massachusetts organizations with documented employer partners demonstrating direct hiring needs. Applicants must incorporate Climatetech Pathmaker Core Competencies and may tailor curriculum to meet specific employer needs. Training is designed to create accelerated pathways to employment for individuals from environmentally burdened or low-income neighborhoods and other underrepresented populations. Eligible applicants are Massachusetts-based community-based organizations, community colleges, universities, post-secondary institutions, vocational high schools, non-profit entities, municipalities, workforce development organizations, and MassHire Workforce Investment Boards and Career Centers. Applicants must have at least one industry partnership; consortiums of multiple industry partners with overlapping workforce needs are also accepted. The program is part of the Healey-Driscoll Administration Economic Development Strategy and is administered by the Massachusetts Executive Office of Economic Development in coordination with the Massachusetts Office of Business Development, Massachusetts Technology Collaborative, Massachusetts Life Sciences Center, and Massachusetts Clean Energy Center.

The MassCEC Pathmaker Climatetech program is an employer-driven workforce development grant that funds short-term, industry-aligned training programs (generally 8-16 weeks, 80-220 hours) to create entry points into Massachusetts' climatetech economy, particularly for individuals without significant industry experience or related postsecondary education, including low-income and underrepresented community members and individuals from Federally recognized or State-acknowledged tribes within the Commonwealth. Applicants must select one of two tracks, Battery Energy Storage Solutions (BESS) Technicians or Power System Technicians, and must have at least one industry employer partner demonstrating direct hiring need, with the option to form a Consortium of multiple industry partners. Programs must incorporate the Pathmaker Core Competencies Checklist (which differs by track and may be amended by MassCEC) while allowing training providers to add employer-responsive curriculum. Funding is evaluated on cost per employment outcome, with $10,000 per employment outcome set as a planning benchmark (all-inclusive of recruitment, training, support, program design, and management); higher costs must be justified for populations needing more intensive services. Eligible uses include staff time, marketing/outreach, subcontracted training delivery, stipends, in-state conference registration, and approved transport; ineligible uses include venue/equipment purchase, capital equipment or infrastructure, proposal preparation costs, pre/post-grant-term activities, individual staff meals, lodging, air travel, alcohol, out-of-state conference costs, and indirect expenses. Funded applicants must contract with the MassHire workforce system for outreach, recruitment, and data collection, and must inform participants they are not employees of the program provider or MassCEC. Awards are disbursed via ACH, with up to 10% available upon grant agreement execution and the remaining 90% reimbursed after invoice submission with supporting documentation. Grantees must track and report enrollment, demographics, languages, completion, placement, six-month retention, and wage change outcomes, submitting progress reports with each invoice and at least monthly; nonperformance can trigger a Go/No-Go corrective action or grant rescission/termination. A successful program is defined as placing at least 60% of the original cohort in relevant climate-critical occupations; placement below 60% may trigger corrective action. Applicants intending to subcontract $50,000 or more must submit a separate detailed subcontractor budget, and cost-sharing (monetary or in-kind, excluding other MassCEC grants) is encouraged and may be prioritized in scoring.

The Cape Cod Foundation offers multiple competitive grant programs for nonprofit organizations serving Cape Cod communities. Programs include Land Acquisition Grants for conservation, Open Door Grants for first-time or recently-unfunded nonprofits, Catalyst Grants for organizational capacity building, Town Fund Grants for specific communities, and Women & Girls Fund Grants. Most programs are currently closed; Town Fund Grants reopen August 4, 2026.

Cape Cod Foundation invests its discretionary funds, professional and staff resources in effective nonprofit organizations and collaboratives serving the Cape Cod region across all areas of community life, including housing, health and human services, education, youth development and recreation, arts and culture, environmental conservation, preservation and restoration, and animals and wildlife. The Foundation prioritizes under-supported areas of the community where needs are great but resources are limited, and favors initiatives with the most profound, systemic, region-wide impact. It funds through fewer, larger grants and multi-year grants, with key investment priorities including filling gaps and meeting unmet needs, replicating successful programs, increasing access to programs and services, building nonprofit capacity, integrating rather than duplicating resources, and promoting collaboration among organizations. The Foundation supports this work through several channels: Competitive Grantmaking Programs for nonprofit programs and capacity-building; over $1.5 million annually in scholarships and related support for local students pursuing post-secondary paths, including emergency assistance for students in urgent need and grants for educational programming; strategic regional partnerships and committee/board participation to leverage resources and shape policy; shared resources such as community forums providing data and education to the nonprofit sector; the Town Fund model, a hyper-local grassroots endowment fund structure combining local Advisory Committee knowledge with Foundation administrative and financial expertise; and replicable philanthropic models such as a 2022 partnership with Southworth Development/Willowbend Country Club for member-driven giving. The Foundation has also run discretionary fundraising initiatives such as the $3.5 Million Community Challenge, the Women and Girls Funds Challenge, and the Strategic Emergency Response Fund established during the pandemic. To date the Foundation has invested more than $113 million in grants and scholarships across the Cape Cod community. This document is an overview of the Foundation's investment strategy rather than a single funding opportunity with specific application details, amounts, or deadlines.

The Cape Cod Foundation makes grants in six program areas, though its grantmaking is not exclusive to these areas: Arts and Culture (expanding access to the arts and providing arts and cultural education and awareness), Children, Youth and Families (increasing access and affordability to programs and services for children and youth, expanding access to resources and education for parents and caregivers, and increasing access to affordable, high-quality childcare and early education), Health and Human Services (expanding access to healthcare and health education, providing behavioral health services including mental health and substance use prevention, treatment and recovery, promoting self-advocacy and self-sufficiency, offering access to healthy nutritional foods, promoting active lifestyles, and supporting individuals with disabilities and their caretakers), Environment (preservation, conservation and restoration of natural resources particularly water and wetlands, public education and outreach on environmental issues, and educational experiences for school-aged children and youth), Community and Economic Development (supporting workforce and career development and training, promoting civic education and engagement, and supporting entrepreneurship), and Housing (promoting attainment and retention of safe, affordable housing, promoting financial literacy and long-term self-sufficiency, and addressing long-term collaborative solutions to the housing crisis on Cape Cod). The document does not specify award amounts, deadlines, eligibility requirements, or application procedures.

The Regional Conservation Partnership Program (RCPP) brings together partners to expand the reach of NRCS conservation programs for agricultural producers and landowners in Massachusetts. The program provides conservation assistance to help farmers, ranchers, and forestland owners conserve natural resources on their operations.

USDA is investing up to $310 Million through the Regional Conservation Partnership Program to boost farm operations and conserve natural resources. 
(WASHINGTON, June 23, 2026) – The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) is putting Farmers First by investing up to $310 million to expand producer conservation activities across the nation through the Regional Conservation Partnership Program (RCPP). USDA’s Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) is accepting RCPP project proposals now through August 24, 2026, to help farmers, ranchers, and forest landowners boost their operations and conserve natural resources. 

“This significant investment through the Regional Conservation Partnership Program will further enable us to leverage our partnerships as force multipliers in supporting America’s farmers,” said NRCS Chief Colton L. Buckley. “We’re looking forward to seeing the results on the ground while we also work to keep working lands in working hands.” 

The Working Families Tax Cuts Act is delivering the largest long-term investment in NRCS conservation programs in decades, including support for RCPP. It will deliver $425 million in fiscal year 2026 and an increase to $450 million from fiscal year 2027 through fiscal year 2031.   

RCPP is a partner-driven approach to conservation that funds solutions to natural resource challenges on agricultural land.  
In the past year, NRCS has improved RCPP, through streamlining partnership agreement processes and increasing flexibilities to ensure the program works more effectively for conservation partners and America’s farmers and ranchers. Now, 75% of the funding goes directly to the American farmer or is used to cover the cost of conservation practice implementation. 

There are two separate funding opportunities:   

RCPP Classic: Projects are implemented using NRCS contracts and easements with producers, landowners and communities in collaboration with project partners.   
RCPP Alternative Funding Arrangements (AFA): The lead partner works directly with agricultural producers to support the development of innovative conservation approaches that would not otherwise be available under RCPP Classic.  
NRCS ranks proposals based on how they address the following priorities:  

Addressing soil health, water quality, or wildlife habitat with an aim to improve land health, enhance resource management, and promote sustainable agriculture and long-term protection of agricultural, grassland, and forestland viability. 
Soil health projects using practices that focus on minimizing soil disturbance, maximizing soil cover, increasing natural vitality, and maintaining living roots throughout the year.  
Leveraging precision agriculture technologies to target conservation efforts based on specific field conditions, potentially reducing costs and improving resource efficiency. 
Focusing on Farmers First projects, especially those that provide technical and financial assistance via contributions for planning and practice designs to support producer contracts. 
Supporting projects led by Indian Tribes.  
More Information 

The $310 million is available for both RCPP Classic and AFA projects, including a $30 million set aside for projects with Indian Tribes. 

Details about RCPP Classic and RCPP AFAs are available on Grants.gov.  Project proposals for RCPP are being accepted through August 24, 2026, on the RCPP portal. For more information about RCPP, visit the RCPP website. 

This investment builds on other recent NRCS investments to engage partners to extend the reach of conservation. In late May, NRCS announced its plans to invest $65 million through Conservation Innovation Grants.  

For more than 90 years, NRCS has helped farmers, ranchers and forestland owners make investments in their operations and local communities to improve the quality of our air, water, soil, and wildlife habitat.  NRCS uses the latest science and technology to help keep working lands working, boost agricultural economies, and increase the competitiveness of American agriculture. NRCS provides one-on-one, personalized advice and financial assistance and works with producers to help them reach their goals through voluntary, incentive-based conservation programs. For more information, visit nrcs.usda.gov.

The Incumbent Worker Training Grant Program helps Rhode Island employers remain competitive by providing 50% to 100% reimbursement for eligible training costs that help workers maintain and advance in their careers. All eligible RI employers may apply with a maximum annual award of $25,000.

REIMBURSEMENT RATES & PROGRAM CAPS
Employers who meet the eligibility criteria outlined above and have 25 or more employees may be
reimbursed at a rate of 50% for eligible costs on eligible training activities. Eligible employers with
fewer than 25 employees may be reimbursed at a higher rate of 75%. 
4
 NEW: Employers of any size may be reimbursed at a rate of 100% for English as a Second
Language Training (otherwise known as ‘ESL On-The-Job’).
The annual award cap for all eligible employers is $25,000 per calendar year. Multiple training
grants may be awarded to an employer until the $25,000 program cap is reached.
Employers with more than one location in Rhode Island may be treated as either one employer or
separate employers depending on the Federal Employer Identification Number(s) (FEINs).
Employers with locations operating under different FEINs will be considered separate entities and
each location may submit its own application(s). Employers with more than one location operating
under a single FEIN are considered one entity.
Reimbursable training dollars are capped at a per-trainee, per year amount of $5,000.
ELIGIBLE TRAINING
Employers may utilize this program to provide training that demonstrates a clear benefit to the
organization and its employee(s). To be approved, an Incumbent Worker Training Grant
Application must demonstrate at least one (1) of the following:
• Training responds to a new or modified local, state, federal, or international regulation or
standard that requires a change in technology, process, etc.
• Training responds to rapidly changing industry practices or skill requirements, new
technologies, or the emergence of new products or competitors.
• New market opportunities may become available because of the skills acquired through
the training.
• The employee(s) will be positioned to advance into higher paying roles because of the
training.
• The employee(s) will receive an industry recognized credential/certification that is
transferable should they separate from the employer.
 NOTE: Provider‑led English as a Second Language (ESL) training that supports workplace
communication and job‑related language skills is also eligible.
Employers may NOT utilize this program to provide training to the following types of personnel:
• Personnel who are not authorized to work in the United States
• Personnel hired as independent contractors under a 1099
• Personnel who are immediate relatives1 of the employer if the immediate relatives are the
only personnel to receive training.
ELIGIBLE COSTS
Costs eligible for reimbursement include:
• Tuition and fees for college courses • Trainers/Instructors (or training provider fees) • Training materials and supplies • Software or subscriptions (if directly related to training and used exclusively for training)
1 An immediate relative is defined as an individual in a person’s family such as a spouse, parent, grandparent, child,
stepchild, sibling, in-law, aunt, uncle, niece, nephew, cousin, or domestic partner. 
5
• Curriculum development (if necessary) • Conference registration fees (see below)
 NOTE: Effective 3/1/2026, conference registration fees are reimbursable only when the
training provided results in a verifiable learning outcome (such as a certificate, credential, or

Point32Health Foundation provides multi-year, general operating grants to nonprofits doing work in aging that addresses equity, especially in communities that have experienced disinvestment and are most affected by systemic barriers. The Foundation operates two grant cycles annually. The first cycle (deadline February 19, 2027) targets organizations working in organizing, policy, advocacy and systems change to improve conditions affecting older adults, with approximately $2M available and likely 4-8 grants per state; decisions announced in June. The second cycle (deadline September 17, 2027) targets organizations working in community building—supporting community power and advancing solutions promoting healthier communities—with approximately $500,000 available and likely 1-3 grants per state; decisions announced in December. General operating grants can be used for traditional operational costs as well as staff wellness, executive leadership coaching, and other capacity building initiatives. The Foundation's fiscal year begins January 1, and approximately 75% of the annual grantmaking budget is already committed to existing grantees. Applicants must submit a short inquiry form; if alignment is found, the Foundation team conducts a conversation to learn more about the organization's work. Recommended organizations are then invited to submit full application documentation. Organizations with active grants seeking renewal do not need to complete the inquiry form. The Foundation serves nonprofits in Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, and Rhode Island.

Point32Health Foundation funds nonprofits in Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, and Rhode Island, the states where Point32Health does business, with a focus on equity in aging. The Foundation invests primarily through general operating and multi-year grants that support upstream, community-led work addressing root causes and social determinants of health for older adults, especially people of color, people with disabilities, and others facing systemic barriers; it does not fund medical care. Funding supports organizing, policy and advocacy, and systems change work (February cycle) or community building, community power, and solutions promoting healthier communities (September cycle). Organizations may submit an inquiry form only once per year for whichever cycle best aligns with their work, and organizations do not hold multiple active grants with the Foundation at once. The annual community investments grantmaking budget is approximately $8 million, of which about 75% is already committed to existing multi-year grantees. It is rare for the Foundation to support a national organization unless the work primarily benefits and is led by people in the four states served. The Foundation also offers sponsorships (reviewed by an enterprise-wide team, rolling basis) and volunteer engagement opportunities (reviewed by the Corporate Citizenship team, rolling basis), which are separate from the grantmaking process.

Point32Health Foundation funds community-led work advancing equity in aging in Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire and Rhode Island, prioritizing efforts that address systemic inequities and advance social and racial justice. The Foundation invests in organizations aligned with two categories: community building and improving conditions for older adults. To receive funding, organizations must support community-based interventions, engage in initiatives with potential to dismantle racist systems, work in communities experiencing historic disinvestment (especially people of color and others facing systemic barriers) while being proximate and connected to the people they serve, use disruptive approaches to influence systems beyond individual organizations, collaborate to expand positive impact, and show promise even if unproven, taking risk. Community building grants must implement a community-led initiative, be led by people connected to the community represented, advance systemic change and fight injustice(s), and work in communities with historic disinvestment and barriers to access. As a core tactic, the Foundation is making a five-year $10 million investment in a set of named intermediary organizations (movement builders proximate to community issues) across the service states. Improving conditions for older adults grants support improving access to nutritious, affordable food, supporting caregivers, providing civic engagement and social connection opportunities, developing community approaches to improved mental health, proposing housing solutions, and devising transportation and community development strategies for older adults. The Foundation does not define 'older people' itself, relying instead on the definitions used by the community organizations it funds. Priorities are reviewed annually.

Overview
EQIP delivers environmental benefits such as improved water and air quality, conserved ground and surface water, increased soil health and reduced soil erosion and sedimentation, improved or created wildlife habitat, and mitigation against drought and increasing weather volatility.

This voluntary conservation programs helps producers make conservation work for them. Together, NRCS and producers invest in solutions that conserve natural resources for the future while also improving agricultural operations. 

Through EQIP, NRCS provides agricultural producers with financial resources and one-on-one help to plan and implement improvements, or what NRCS calls conservation practices. Using these practices can lead to cleaner water and air, healthier soil and better wildlife habitat, all while improving agricultural operations. Through EQIP, you can voluntarily implement conservation practices, and NRCS co-invests in these practices with you.

How It Works
This voluntary conservation programs helps producers make conservation work for them.  Together, NRCS and producers invest in solutions that conserve natural resources for the future while also improving agricultural operations.

Through EQIP, NRCS provides agricultural producers and non-industrial forest managers with financial resources and one-on-one help to plan and implement improvements, or what NRCS calls conservation practices.  Using these practices can lead to cleaner water and air, healthier soil and better wildlife habitat, all while improving agricultural operations.  Through EQIP, you can voluntarily implement conservation practices, and NRCS co-invests in these practices with you.

To get started, NRCS first works one-on-one with you to develop a conservation plan that meets your goals and vision for the land. This becomes a roadmap for which conservation practices best meet your needs. 

Financial assistance covers part of the costs from implementing conservation practices. NRCS offers about 200 practices depending on where your land is located. These practices are geared towards working farms, ranches and forests and provide producers with many options for conservation. See a list of practices. 

Benefits
The benefits of EQIP include:

Reduction of contamination from agricultural sources, such as animal feeding operations.
Efficient utilization of nutrients, reducing input costs and reduction in nonpoint source pollution.
Increased soil health to help mitigate against increasing weather volatility and improved drought resiliency.
How to Apply
The best way to learn if EQIP is a good fit for you is by contacting your local NRCS office. If you choose to move forward, your local NRCS conservationist will guide you through applying for the program. 

Applications are ranked, and if yours is funded, NRCS will offer you an EQIP contract to receive financial assistance for the cost of implementing practices. Payment rates for conservation practices are reviewed and set each fiscal year. More information on this process is available on our How Do I Apply webpage; new-to-NRCS producers will find specific guidance for establishing farm records (Farm & Tract Number), initiating the Highly Erodible Land and Wetland Compliance evaluation, updating Adjusted Gross Income, etc.

Program Priorities
National priorities
The national priorities include soil quality, water quality and quantity, plants, energy, wildlife habitat, air
quality, increased weather volatility, and related natural resource concerns:

Reductions of nonpoint source pollution, such as nutrients, sediment, pesticides, or excess salinity in
impaired watersheds consistent with total maximum daily loads (TMDL) where available;
The reduction of surface and ground water contamination;
The reduction of contamination from agricultural sources, such as animal feeding operations;
Conservation of ground and surface water resources, including improvement of irrigation efficiency;
Reduction of emissions, such as particulate matter, nitrogen oxides, volatile organic compounds, and
ozone precursors and depleters that contribute to air quality impairment violations of the National AmbientAir Quality Standards;
Reduction in soil erosion and sedimentation from unacceptable levels on eligible land;
Promotion of at-risk species habitat conservation including development and improvement of wildlife
habitat; and
Energy conservation to help save fuel, improve efficiency of water use, maintain production, and protect
soil and water resources by more efficiently using fertilizers and pesticides.
State Priorities
Massachusetts top priorities include water quality and quantity, soil health, invasive plants, and wildlife habitat:

Impaired waters (categories 5-4)
Drinking water (groundwater zones 1-2; surface water zones a-b)
Water conservation (stressed basins)
Soil quality and soil health
Invasive Plant Species
At-risk-species habitat conservation

The John A. McNeice Jr. Charitable Foundation is a private foundation based in Boston, Massachusetts. Guided by its grantor's wishes, it supports the Roman Catholic Church and Church related charitable, educational, and medical organizations. Its funding priorities are the Catholic faith and mission of the Catholic Church, the education, training, and development, both spiritual and intellectual, of young people, and those who are unable to support themselves. It funds public charities, rarely outside Massachusetts, and does not fund efforts to build up endowments or other investments, or consistent, permanent annual funding. Grants generally range from $25,000 to $250,000 per year, and the foundation gave $4,418,950 in 2024. Interested applicants request a preliminary application from the foundation's website, complete and return it by the end of the first month of a four month review cycle (October through January or April through July), and if invited, submit a final application by the end of the third month. John A. McNeice, Jr., the Grantor of the Foundation, offered the following guidance to the trustees of the Foundation, for determining whether to approve a distribution: " ... distributions primarily to the Roman Catholic Church and Church related charitable, educational, and medical organizations ... more specifically, to support and promote (1) the Catholic faith and mission of the Catholic Church; (2) the education, training, and development, both spiritual and intellectual, of young people; (3) those who are unable to support themselves." Trustees will first ensure that requests comply with the above statement by the Grantor. Grant applications are reviewed on the schedule below. If an application deadline falls on a weekend, then the applications are due by 5 p.m. ET on the Friday immediately preceding the deadline. Two (2) rounds of awards are reviewed each year, according to the following schedule. Each round is a 4-consecutive month process, as follows: October, November, December, and January; April, May, June, and July. Month #1: Applicant accesses the mcneicefoundation.org link, and requests a “preliminary” application, completes it, and returns it by the end of month #1. To request the “preliminary” application, click here. If the link does not work for you, please email mcneicefoundation@choate.com and request a link to the “preliminary” application. Month #2: Trustees and their advisors review the “preliminary” applications, and the Trustees then decide by the end of month #2 which applicants should be invited to submit “final” applications. Month #3: Invited applicants complete and file a “final” application by the end of month #3. Month #4: Trustees decide which “final” applications will be given awards, and the amounts and payment dates thereof. Enter the following information on the online form: A brief description of the organization. A description of the project or need. A budget for the project with any transaction costs broken down. The Trustees will not approve grant requests seeking funds to reimburse the applicant for building up endowments or other investments. The contact person for the organization and the email address provided must be the person responsible for the application and for any follow-up to the Preliminary Application. Those applicants that are chosen to submit a Final Application will be invited via email, there will not be a mailed invitation. The applicant will receive an automated email confirming the preliminary application was submitted successfully online. If you do not receive a confirmation email, please contact mcneicefoundation@choate.com to confirm we have received your application. STAGE TWO: Final Application (by invitation only) Description of the project or need: What will be accomplished? Does your project have a reasonable assurance of success? Ability to carry the project through:
When do you plan to start the project, and what contingencies, if any, could affect this timing? What are the qualifications of the person(s) responsible for implementation? Will a McNeice Foundation grant “make or break” the project? What criteria will be used to measure success? In due course, will you provide the Trustees with an objective appraisal of the project’s success? REQUIRED ATTACHMENTS – IN THIS ORDER
Project budget – provide a thorough breakdown of project costs and funding
Board of Trustees/Directors
Financials
IRS Determination Letter
Resume of primary person overseeing the project
Other attachments – if applicable
In addition to the online Final Application form, please mail one single-sided paper copy of the Final Application, along with all required attachments. Please do not include staples, bindings, brochures, or items that differ from those listed above. Completed materials should be mailed to the address listed below. John A. What is CSP? The Conservation Stewardship Program (CSP) offers technical and financial assistance to help agricultural and forest producers take their conservation efforts to the next level. The program is designed to compensate agricultural and forest producers who agree to increase their level of conservation by adopting additional conservation activities and maintaining their baseline level of conservation. CSP is for producers who are passionate about conservation and environmental stewardship. What are the Benefts? CSP may provide many benefits, including increased crop productivity, decreased inputs, wildlife habitat improvements and increased resilience to weather extremes. CSP also encourages adoption of new technologies and management techniques. For example, CSP can help you: Schedule timely planting and management of cover crops Develop a grazing plan that will improve your forage base Implement no-till to reduce erosion or manage forested areas in a way that benefits wildlife habitat If you are already taking steps to improve the condition of the land, chances are CSP can help you find new ways to meet your goals. How Does CSP Work? CSP offers opportunities for producers to expand on existing conservation efforts by applying new conservation practices, enhancements, and bundles. These new activities will help enhance natural resources and improve the operation. For example, if you have been planting a cover crop, you may decide to try an enhancement for a multi-species cover crop or implement a deep rooted cover crop to break up soil compaction. If you decide to apply for CSP, the local NRCS conservation planner will have a one-on-one consultation with you to evaluate your current management system and the natural resources on your land. You will then work with the NRCS conservation planner to select new CSP conservation activities based on your management objectives for your operation. Once you choose the conservation practices or activities that best fit, and if your application is selected for funding, CSP offers annual payments for implementing these practices on your land, and operating and maintaining existing conservation efforts. 

The Conservation Stewardship Program (CSP) helps you build on your existing conservation efforts while strengthening your operation. 

Whether you are looking to improve grazing conditions, increase crop resiliency, or develop wildlife habitat, we can custom design a CSP plan to help you meet those goals. We can help you identify natural resource problems in your operation and provide technical and financial assistance to solve those problems or attain higher stewardship levels in an environmentally beneficial and cost-effective manner.

How It Works
If you are already taking steps to improve the condition of the land, chances are, CSP can help you find new ways to meet your goals.

NRCS works one-on-one with producers to develop a conservation plan that outlines and enhances existing efforts, using new conservation practices or activities, based on management objectives for your operation. Producers implement practices and activities in their conservation plan that expands on the benefits of cleaner water and air, healthier soil and better wildlife habitat, all while improving their agricultural operations. 

For example, if you have been planting a cover crop, you may decide to try an enhancement for a multi-species cover crop or implement a deep-rooted cover crop to break up soil compaction and further improve the health of your soil.

CSP offers annual payments for implementing these practices on your land and operating and maintaining existing conservation efforts. Want to take it a step further? CSP also offers bundles where you can select a suite of enhancements and receive a higher payment rate.

Benefits
CSP is for working lands and is the largest conservation program in the United States. Thousands of people voluntarily enroll in the program because it helps them enhance natural resources and improve their business operation.

CSP participants are seeing real results.  Some of these benefits include:

Enhanced resiliency to weather and market volatility
Decreased need for agricultural inputs
Improved wildlife habitat conditions

The program represents a genuine commitment to conservation – CSP contracts are for five years, with the opportunity to compete for a contract renewal if you successfully fulfill the initial contract and agree to achieve additional conservation objectives. text: The Colorado Organizational Resiliency (COR) program provides grants to nonprofit organizations serving older adults in Colorado to build economic resilience and organizational capacity. text: Cummings Foundation Grants Inc is a private foundation based in Woburn, Massachusetts, founded by Joyce and Bill Cummings to direct the profits of their commercial real estate business toward charitable causes in the communities where the business operates. Its Cummings $35 Million Grant Program supports Human services, Fairness and justice, Education, Healthcare, and The Environment. The foundation funds public charities headquartered in and primarily serving the 12 Massachusetts cities and towns where Cummings Properties operates commercial real estate (with a related interest in Rwanda through a partnership with Partners In Health), and it does not generally fund endowments, medical research, private foundations, religious endeavors, political or lobbying organizations, or organizations already supported by large endowments, among others. Most grants are three-year awards of $30,000 to $300,000, with a smaller number of ten-year grants up to $1,000,000 and annual installments ranging from $10,000 to $100,000; according to its 2024 tax filing it gave $38,223,794 that year. Nonprofits apply by submitting a letter of inquiry through the foundation's online portal, following the guidelines and deadlines posted on its website.

text: This grant program from Berkshire Taconic Community Foundation funds projects that increase access to fresh and healthy food in Columbia County, particularly for food-insecure households with limited resources. Eligible applicants include Columbia County food pantries and food distribution sites, farmers markets, schools, nonprofit organizations with 501(c)(3) status, public agencies, and fiscally sponsored organizations. Grants range up to $7,500. A portion of available funds is specifically set aside for community refrigerator projects. Eligible projects include market match/double up programs at farmers markets, healthy corner store initiatives, food pantry needs, gleaning programs, subsidized CSA shares, and other innovative ideas focused on increasing access to fresh and healthy food. Applications are reviewed based on impact (potential impact, innovation, and whether it increases access to fresh and healthy food for those most in need), feasibility (applicant capacity and cost-effectiveness), and geographic benefit (extent to which the project benefits areas where food-insecure and low-income households are concentrated, and whether it addresses immediate or long-term community needs). The foundation does not support organizations that discriminate based on age, race, national origin, ethnicity, gender, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, political affiliation, or religious belief.

text: Wellington Management Foundation is a corporate foundation based in Boston, Massachusetts, created in 1992 by Wellington Management, with a mission to close the opportunity and achievement gap in education for youth in historically underserved communities. Its funding priorities are Thriving communities, which supports educational and life-skills programs such as academic improvement, educational transitions, extended learning time, and career readiness for youth up to age 26, and Effective operational stewards, which focuses on sustainability within the firm's own operations, including energy use, carbon neutrality, travel, and supply chain. It funds not-for-profit organizations serving low-income youth in eastern Massachusetts, the greater Philadelphia area, Chicago, the San Francisco Bay area, Toronto, Tokyo, Hong Kong, Singapore, and Sydney, as well as, through its UK Foundation, organizations registered and operating in the UK, Germany, Switzerland, Luxembourg, Italy, and Spain; it does not fund scholarship programs and does not accept unsolicited proposals for catalyst gifts or strategic partnerships. A typical grant is $60,000, and the foundation gave $4,970,000 according to its 2024 tax filing. The foundation's application process is by invitation only, with its US review committee beginning its cycle in September and disbursing grants in December, while its UK funding cycle typically begins in April with grants usually dispersed in September; multi-year grants are considered once a relationship with a grantee is established.

text: The Memorial Foundation for the Blind Inc is a private foundation based in Worcester, Massachusetts, whose mission is to serve the needs and promote the general welfare of visually impaired residents of Worcester County. Its funding priorities include Operating Grants to lead agencies providing direct services to blind and visually impaired individuals, Program Grants for proposals that improve quality of life and independence (such as access to arts and culture, employment training, and recreation), Individual Grants for assistive technology, equipment, or training and education fees, and Scholarships for higher education. The foundation funds nonprofit organizations serving Worcester County as well as individual legally blind residents of that county's cities and towns, and it does not accept unsolicited proposals for operating grants. Individual grants are limited to a maximum of $3,000 over a three-year period, and scholarships may be awarded up to $3,000 per year; according to its 2025 tax filing, a typical grant is $120,000 and total giving that year was $388,029. The foundation accepts applications year-round for individual grants, requires a brief letter of intent for program grant proposals, and sets scholarship applications due by April 1, while general grant applications must be received seven days before the monthly board meeting (the board does not meet in summer).

text: The Sontag Foundation is a private foundation based in Ponte Vedra Beach, Florida, that invests in scientists working to advance brain cancer research and treatment breakthroughs. It funds public charities, chiefly research institutions and universities, with notable giving concentrated in Florida, Massachusetts, California, Texas, Pennsylvania, New York, and Illinois. Grants under its main research programs typically run from $38,000 to $150,000 per year, with restrictions capping some awards at a maximum of $600,000, and the foundation gave $7,153,332 in 2024. Applicants for the Distinguished Scientist Award and Career Development Grants must apply online in response to published requests for applications, with the 2026 application portal opening January 12, 2026, and a deadline of March 18, 2026.

text: Cleveland H. The foundation funds public charities primarily in the New York City metropolitan area, and it does not fund individuals, endowments, hospitals or medical research, universities or independent schools (except existing legacy relationships), or organizations outside the New York City area (except legacy relationships), among others, nor political campaigns or lobbying. text: The Lawson Valentine Foundation is a private, family foundation based in Princeton, NJ, that works to advance racial justice by supporting grassroots organizing, advocacy, and policy work on behalf of people of color, low-income youth, immigrants, refugees, and other underserved populations.
